# Application: admissions and dismissals in Brazil {#sec-application}

## Data

Brazil's General Register of Employed and Unemployed (CAGED) records every admission and dismissal of formally employed workers.
The two variables share a geographical hierarchy: 26 states and the Federal District (27 federative units) aggregate to five regions, which aggregate to the country (@fig-map).
So $m = 2$, $n = 33$ and $n_b = 27$, giving 66 series in all.

```{r}
#| label: fig-map
#| fig-cap: "Brazilian regions and federative units."
#| out-width: 14.5cm

knitr::include_graphics(tar_read(fig_region_map))
```

The Labour Statistics Dissemination Program (PDET) of the Ministry of Labour and Employment publishes monthly counts of admissions and dismissals by federative unit, without seasonal adjustment.

In January 2020 CAGED was replaced by Novo CAGED, which draws on different administrative sources, and the COVID-19 pandemic began soon after.
Both events changed the joint behaviour of admissions and dismissals, and would contaminate an estimate of their forecast error covariance.
We therefore use only January 2004 to December 2019 (192 months).

@fig-app-data shows the national series.
Admissions and dismissals move together, with strong seasonality: December brings large net job losses every year.
Net employment change was positive until 2014, negative through the recession of 2015--2017, and positive again from 2018.

```{r}
#| label: fig-app-data
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Monthly admissions, dismissals and net employment change in Brazil.
#| out-width: 100%

knitr::include_graphics(tar_read(fig_data))
```

## Forecasting set-up

We forecast all 66 series from rolling origins with an expanding window.
The first origin has 108 months of training data (January 2004 to December 2012), and each later origin adds one month.
This gives `r num$appOrigins` origins, `r num$appOriginsFull` of which have all twelve horizons within the sample.
There are two sets of base forecasts.
The first comes from an ARIMA model selected automatically for each series [@hyndman2021forecasting].
The second comes from a bivariate VAR for admissions and dismissals at each node, with no seasonal terms and a lag order of up to five selected by the AICc.
Results for ETS base forecasts are in the Supplementary Material.
We compare the base forecasts with OLS, structurally weighted least squares (WLS) and MinT reconciliation.
MinT is applied in three ways: separately to each variable, jointly to both, and separately using the diagonal blocks of the joint covariance estimate.
The third isolates the effect of the cross-variable blocks from that of the different shrinkage intensities of the separate and joint estimates.

## Diagnostics

@tbl-app-diag reports diagnostics computed from the one-step residuals of models fitted to the whole of 2004--2019.
For the ARIMA base forecasts, the estimated error covariance is close to separable: the relative error of the nearest Kronecker product is `r num$appKronArima`.
Joint reconciliation would place moderate weight on the other variable's incoherences ($\widehat\kappa = `r num[["appKappaArima"]]`$), but the plug-in gain in mean squared error is only `r num$appGainArima`%.
The incoherences account for `r num$appIncohArima`% of the total variance of the one-step errors.
The likelihood ratio test rejects the conditions of @prp-equivalence ($p `r num$appPTextArima`$), so the departure is small but not pure estimation noise.
The test assumes serially uncorrelated residuals, however, and a Ljung--Box test with 24 lags rejects at the 5% level for `r num$appLbArima`% of the ARIMA residual series, so the $p$-value is only indicative.
The VAR residuals give a larger $\widehat\kappa$ (`r num$appKappaVar`) and larger $F$ statistics.
But they are autocorrelated for `r num$appLbVar`% of the series, which invalidates the test: with no seasonal terms and at most five lags, the per-node VARs cannot capture the annual seasonality.

For net employment change the plug-in gain is larger.
With $\bm{\ell}$ selecting admissions minus dismissals at a node, $\widehat\gamma_{\bm{\ell}}$ is `r num$appNetPlugTotal`% for the national net change and, on average, `r num$appNetPlugRegions`% for the regions and `r num$appNetPlugStates`% for the states.

::: {#tbl-app-diag}
```{r}
#| output: asis

cat(readLines(tar_read(table_app_diag)), sep = "\n")
```

Application: diagnostics from the one-step residuals over 2004--2019.
Estimated $\widehat\kappa$ and plug-in gain $\widehat\gamma$ (%); Rao $F$ statistics for the other variable's incoherences in the regression of each variable's errors (`r num$appDfOneArima` and `r num$appDfTwoArima` degrees of freedom for ARIMA, `r num$appDfOneVar` and `r num$appDfTwoVar` for VAR), and the Bonferroni $p$-value; incoherence variance ratio $\operatorname{tr}(\bm{C}_*\bm{W}\bm{C}_*')/\operatorname{tr}(\bm{W})$ (%); relative error of the nearest Kronecker product.
:::

## Forecast accuracy

@tbl-app-accuracy-arima gives the mean squared error of each method relative to the ARIMA base forecasts.
For admissions, separate MinT reconciliation improves on the base forecasts at every level.
It also beats OLS and structural WLS, which both damage the state-level forecasts.

For dismissals, separate MinT does worse.
At the national level its mean squared error is `r num$appSepDisTotalLoss`% higher than that of the base forecasts, and higher than that of OLS and structural WLS.
It is worse than the base forecasts at `r num$appSepDisWorseShare`% of the origins, so a few unusual months are not the cause.
The reason is that the national ARIMA models forecast dismissals well: summing the state base forecasts gives a mean squared error `r num$appBottomUpDisLoss`% higher than the national base forecast.
MinT shifts weight towards the state-level forecasts, which for dismissals is the wrong direction.

Joint reconciliation recovers part of that loss.
For dismissals it beats separate MinT at every level, with ratios of mean squared errors in the range `r num$appJointSepArimaDis`, and the gain holds at every horizon (Supplementary Table\ S3).
For admissions it is slightly worse (`r num$appJointSepArimaAdm`).
The gain for dismissals is larger than the plug-in gain of `r num$appGainArima`% would suggest.

The results depend on the base model.
With VAR base forecasts (@tbl-app-accuracy-var), joint reconciliation is worse than separate reconciliation at every level (ratios `r num$appJointSepVarRange`).
The VAR base forecasts are also poorer to begin with: on average over the series, their mean squared error is `r num$appVarVsArimaBase`% higher than that of the ARIMA base forecasts.
With ETS base forecasts (Supplementary Table\ S2), joint reconciliation is better for dismissals (`r num$appJointSepEtsDis`) and neutral for admissions (`r num$appJointSepEtsAdm`).
So the benefit for dismissals appears where separate reconciliation is itself poor.

::: {#tbl-app-accuracy-arima}

```{r}
cat(readLines(tar_read(table_app_arima)), sep = "\n")
```

## Net employment change

Net employment change is a linear combination of the two variables, so the argument of @sec-theory suggests that joint reconciliation may help it by more than it helps either variable alone.
@tbl-app-prob shows that it does at the national and regional levels.
Compared with separate reconciliation, joint reconciliation reduces the mean squared error of net change by `r num$appNetPointTotal`% at the national level, `r num$appNetPointRegions`% for the regions and `r num$appNetPointStates`% for the states.
It makes the errors in admissions and dismissals more positively correlated, so more of the error cancels in the difference.
Pooled over all series and horizons, their correlation is `r num$appErrCorJoint` after joint reconciliation and `r num$appErrCorSep` after separate reconciliation.
Almost all of the gain comes from the cross-variable blocks.
The different shrinkage intensity of the joint covariance estimate contributes little: separate reconciliation with the joint estimate reduces the mean squared error by at most `r num$appNetShrinkMax`%.

For probabilistic forecasts, we generated 1000 sample paths of all 66 series at each origin from the fitted ARIMA models, driven by resampled one-step residuals, and reconciled every path [@panagiotelis2023probabilistic].
Resampling each variable's innovations independently discards the dependence between admissions and dismissals, while resampling whole residual vectors keeps it.
With separate reconciliation, keeping the dependence reduces the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) of net change by `r num$appNetJointSepTotal`% nationally, `r num$appNetJointSepRegions`% for the regions and `r num$appNetJointSepStates`% for the states.
Reconciling the paths jointly raises the reduction to `r num$appNetJointJointTotal`% nationally and `r num$appNetJointJointRegions`% for the regions.

::: {#tbl-app-prob}
```{r}

cat(readLines(tar_read(table_app_prob)), sep = "\n")
```

Application: forecasts of net employment change (admissions minus dismissals), ARIMA base models, geometric mean over the series at each level, `r num$appOrigins` origins (`r num$appOriginsFull` with all twelve horizons), horizons 1--12.
Top: MSE of point forecasts relative to separate MinT.
Bottom: CRPS from 1000 sample paths relative to independent innovations with separate reconciliation.
